title: Ashtpadi 24, salok: the perfect Lord
hook: pooraa prabh aaraadhiaa: I worshiped the perfect Lord (Sukhmani 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pargaas, and your line: see freshly. Did you spot something new on a familiar route? Today Sukhmani reaches its last ashtpadi, the twenty-fourth. Day five hundred thirty.

Listen to how often you say perfect in a day. The barista asks if oat milk is okay: perfect. A coworker says the meeting moved to three: perfect. Your friend says she's running ten minutes late: perfect. We've worn the word down until it means fine, or got it, or sure. Sukhmani's twenty-fourth ashtpadi opens with that same word, pooraa, four times in two short lines. And it means it, every time.
screen: `OAT MILK? PERFECT.` → `A WORD WORN DOWN TO FINE.` → `POORAA, FOUR TIMES.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: I worshiped the perfect Lord, whose Name is perfect. Nanak has found the perfect One; sing the praises of the perfect One. Pooraa means full, complete, whole, lacking nothing. A pooraa glass is filled to the top. A pooraa job is finished. When Gurbani calls God pooraa, it means nothing in God is missing or partial, and nothing needs to be added. Count the word as it goes: the perfect Lord, the perfect Name, the perfect One found, the perfect One praised. It's like a bell rung four times. And look at the order. First, aaraadhiaa: I worshiped, I remembered with devotion. Then paaiaa: I found, I attained. Then the invitation: gaau, sing. Worship leads to finding; finding spills over into song. That's the whole of Sukhmani in miniature. It's fitting that this is the last salok. Over twenty-three ashtpadis, Sukhmani has walked through nearly everything a life holds: pride and humility, slander and praise, wealth that stays behind, the wanderer at the door, the stillness before creation, the eye-ointment of wisdom. Now, at the end, it gathers all of that into one word. Not a summary of the argument, a word of praise. After all the teaching, what's left here is gratitude, sung. The word we've worn down to fine gets its weight back here. Full, whole, lacking nothing. In these two short lines, only one thing is called that, four times running.
screen: `POORAA: FULL, WHOLE, LACKING NOTHING.` · `FOUR TIMES, LIKE A BELL.` · `WORSHIP, THEN FINDING, THEN SONG.` · `THE LAST SALOK GATHERS IT ALL.` · then, large: `THE PERFECT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise once. Sit quietly and let one thing come to mind that's full and good: a person's kindness, a view, a piece of music, the fact of your own breathing. Stay with it until gratitude rises on its own. Then let it out once, in a single word or phrase, quietly or aloud. If you pray, the word can be Waheguru, which itself is a word of wonder and praise. Then rest in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Pooraa, full, perfect, complete: its salok rings pooraa four times: the perfect Lord, the perfect Name, the perfect One found, the perfect One praised.
Your line: the perfect one. Today, each time you say perfect out of habit, let it remind you of the One the salok means. Day five hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting the final ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib begin with a salok that names God pooraa, perfect and whole, four times, moving from worship to finding to song.

myth: the twenty-fourth salok uses the word pooraa four times
the perfect Lord, Name, One found, and One praised.
the last salok sums up Sukhmani with an argument
pooraa in Gurbani means roughly fine, or okay
it means full, complete, lacking nothing.

fork.setup: you've walked all twenty-three ashtpadis. the salok moves worship, finding, then what?
options: song: sing the praises of the perfect One.
fork.reveal: gaau: sing. finding the perfect One spills over into praise, which is how Sukhmani's last salok ends.

original.note: Gurmukhi: pooraa, full, perfect, complete; rung four times in the last salok.

trapdoor: what you thought: the perfect Lord means a God who never makes mistakes.
what it means: God is pooraa, whole and lacking nothing, and finding that One spills over into song.
what a scholar hears: the salok's verbs move aaraadhiaa, paaiaa, gaau, worshiped, found, sing, from past devotion to a present invitation.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 24, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 295)

notes: Audit (second sample): removed two unsourced sweeping lines ('Sikh teaching tends to end that way'; 'only one thing in Sukhmani is called that four times running', which overreached since pooraa recurs through the ashtpadi) and kept the claim to the salok itself.
Paraphrase of the ashtpadi 24 salok (pooraa prabh aaraadhiaa pooraa jaa kaa naau; naanak pooraa paaiaa poore ke gun gaau): confirm; note the fourth form is poore, the same word inflected.
Ang 295 for the opening of ashtpadi 24: confirm.
Waheguru glossed as a word of wonder and praise: standard.
